params.why: keeps the area of triangle SNT a whole number of cm squared

stem: In $\triangle MNR$, $\hat{M} = 90^{\circ}$. $S$ is the mid-point of $MN$ and $T$ is the mid-point of $NR$, and $ST$ is drawn. $ST = {=a}$ cm and the area of $\triangle SNT$ is ${=area}$ cm$^{2}$. Calculate the area of quadrilateral $MSTR$ in cm$^{2}$.
solution: $S$ is the mid-point of $MN$ and $T$ is the mid-point of $NR$, so $ST \parallel MR$ and $ST = \frac{1}{2}MR$ (mid-point theorem).
$N\hat{S}T = \hat{M} = 90^{\circ}$ (corresp $\angle$s; $ST \parallel MR$), so $\triangle SNT$ has a right angle at $S$ and its area is $\frac{1}{2} \times ST \times SN$.
${=area} = \frac{1}{2}({=a}) \times SN$, so $SN = \frac{2 \times {=area}}{{=a}} = {=b}$ cm. $S$ is the mid-point of $MN$, so $MN = 2 \times {=b} = {=2 * b}$ cm.
Area of $\triangle MNR = \frac{1}{2} \times MR \times MN = \frac{1}{2}({=2 * a})({=2 * b}) = {=2 * a * b}$ cm$^{2}$.
Area of $MSTR$ = area of $\triangle MNR$ $-$ area of $\triangle SNT = {=2 * a * b} - {=area} = {=3 * area}$ cm$^{2}$.
notes: Extends book ex12-2-6b (p. 412) by one step: the book asks for the area of the whole right-angled triangle, this asks for the quadrilateral MSTR left after cutting off triangle SNT. The book's figure (triangle MNP with R on MP, T the intersection of SU and NR) is restated in words: right angle at M, S mid-point of MN, T mid-point of NR, ST drawn, so a blind solver needs no diagram. Only the book's own method is used: mid-point theorem (ST parallel to MR and ST = half of MR), corresponding angles to get the right angle at S, area = half x base x height. The geometry is consistent for every instance (right triangle SNT with legs ST = a and SN = b gives MN = 2b, MR = 2a, area MNR = 4 x area SNT), so the answer is always 3 x area SNT. A solver who prefers the area-ratio shortcut reaches the same value. a and b are drawn so a*b is even (area stays a whole number); about 44 distinct (ST, area) pairs, max answer 108.
